title: 6-7, rizz and rage bait: decoding the words of the year
description: Every year the big English dictionaries each pick a Word of the Year, and lately the winners come from TikTok and AI. This quiz covers the winners announced for 2023 to 2025: what they mean, where they came from and who picked them. The explanations also show how the dictionaries choose, mostly from search and usage data, with a public vote at Oxford.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: In 2025, a student answers "How was the test?" with "6-7" and a palms-up hand gesture. What do they mean?

options.text: Something like "so-so" or "maybe this, maybe that", or nothing at all
They scored 6 or 7 out of 10
It's a countdown to the end of the lesson
It's code for "I'll tell you later"

questions.explanation:
6-7 has no fixed meaning. The gesture, both palms up and bobbing up and down like a pair of scales, suggests "so-so" or "could go either way", and some people use it that way. Just as often it means nothing, and kids shout it whenever a 6 or a 7 comes up. Dictionary.com called it "meaningless, ubiquitous, and nonsensical", and Skrilla, whose song started it, has said he never gave it a meaning.

The phrase is still useful to the kids who say it. Knowing when to say it, and laughing when someone else does, shows you're part of the group. Asking what it means, as many adults do, shows you're not.

questions.title: Where did "6-7" come from?

options.text: A rap song, "Doot Doot (6 7)" by Skrilla
An episode of *South Park*
A maths-class joke that 6 × 7 = 42, the "answer to everything"
A dance challenge started by a TikTok brand account

questions.explanation:
It comes from the chorus of Skrilla's drill track "Doot Doot (6 7)", released in December 2024. Fans then set the song to basketball highlight clips, a March 2025 video of a boy yelling it at a game went viral, and searches for it climbed from June.

*South Park* came later. Its season 28 premiere on 15 October 2025 built a plot around kids brainwashed by the meme, so the phrase was already famous enough to parody. The *Hitchhiker's Guide* joke is a coincidence. Nobody connected 6-7 to 42.

images.alt: Vertical timeline of how 6-7 went from a rap song to Word of the Year. December 2024: Skrilla releases the drill track Doot Doot (6 7). Next: fan edits pair it with LaMelo Ball, listed at 6 feet 7 inches. March 2025: a clip of a boy yelling it at a basketball game goes viral. Summer 2025: searches for 67 grow more than sixfold after June. 15 October 2025: South Park's season 28 premiere parodies it. 29 October 2025, highlighted: Dictionary.com names 67 its 2025 Word of the Year.

questions.title: Why is NBA player LaMelo Ball part of the 6-7 story?

options.text: He is listed at 6 feet 7 inches tall
He wears the number 67
He once scored 67 points in a game
He recorded the song with Skrilla

questions.explanation:
LaMelo Ball is listed at 6 ft 7 in (2.01 m). Fans cut his highlights to the "6 7" line in Skrilla's song, and that height pun tied the number to basketball.

The number in the song had nothing to do with basketball. The fan edits gave it a second setting and a new audience: basketball fans.

questions.title: Dictionary.com named "67" its 2025 Word of the Year. What evidence showed its editors that the number itself was trending?

options.text: Searches for 67 grew more than sixfold after June 2025, while most other two-digit numbers showed no trend
A public vote in which 67 beat every other shortlisted word
Teachers sent in more complaints about it than about any other word
It appeared in more printed books in 2025 than any new word

questions.explanation:
Dictionary.com's editors checked headlines, social media trends and search data. Searches for 67 rose more than sixfold after June 2025. The strongest evidence was the comparison with other two-digit numbers, most of which showed no real trend over the same months. On its own, a jump in searches for a number could come from homework, sports scores or noise. Next to the flat numbers, the jump clearly belonged to 67.

The public vote is Oxford's method. Printed books lag far behind slang, so Word of the Year teams rely on web and search data instead. Dictionary.com's 2025 shortlist also included *agentic*, *aura farming*, *clanker* and *tariff*. A number is an odd winner, so the announcement included a section on what counts as a word.
questions.references: [Dictionary.com: 2025 Word of the Year](https://www.dictionary.com/articles/word-of-the-year-2025), [CBS News: Dictionary.com picks 67](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dictionary-67-2025-word-of-the-year-meaning/)

questions.title: In 2025, many schools told students to stop saying "6-7". Why?

options.text: Students shouted it, with the gesture, whenever a 6 or a 7 came up, and it derailed lessons
It was a hidden code for sharing test answers
It has an offensive meaning
The song it comes from was banned from radio

questions.explanation:
The bans were about disruption. Numbers come up all the time in school: page 67, question 6, a 6 on the board in maths. Each one set off a chorus of "six-seven!" with the hand gesture. Dictionary.com reported that teachers were soon swapping tips online on how to stop students saying it all day.

None of the other answers has any basis. The phrase has no hidden or offensive meaning. The joke is the interruption itself.

questions.title: Which longer word was shortened to give us "rizz"?
questions.description: Rizz means style, charm or attractiveness, especially the ability to attract a romantic partner.

options.text: Charisma
Rizzo, a character in *Grease*
Risqué
Rising

questions.explanation:
Rizz comes from the middle of *cha-RIS-ma*. Linguists call this clipping: making a new word by cutting down an old one. Most clippings keep the front, as in *lab* from *laboratory*, or the back, as in *phone* from *telephone*. Keeping the middle is rarer. *Flu* from *influenza* is the best-known example, and rizz is another.

The double *z* works like the one in *jazz* and *fizz*. It keeps the vowel short, so the word rhymes with *fizz*, not *rise*.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/), [Wikipedia: Clipping (morphology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipping_(morphology))

questions.title: In which year did Oxford name "rizz" its Word of the Year?
questions.explanation:
Oxford picked rizz for 2023. More than 30,000 people voted in head-to-head rounds that cut eight shortlisted words down to four finalists: *rizz*, *Swiftie*, *situationship* and *prompt*. Oxford's lexicographers then chose the winner using the vote and their usage data.

*Prompt*, the instruction you give an AI model, was already a finalist in 2023. Two years later, AI words won at three dictionaries.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/)

questions.title: Oxford's 2024 Word of the Year was first recorded in Henry David Thoreau's *Walden* (1854). Type the two-word term.
questions.description: Thoreau asked: "While England endeavors to cure the potato-rot, will not any endeavor to cure the ______, which prevails so much more widely and fatally?"
questions.explanation:
It's *brain rot*. Thoreau used it to complain that his society valued simple ideas over complex ones. So the first recorded use of a word many people credit to TikTok is in a book from 1854.

Oxford defines brain rot as the supposed deterioration of a person's mental state from consuming too much trivial material, "now particularly online content". More than 37,000 people voted on the 2024 shortlist, and Oxford's data showed usage up 230% from 2023 to 2024. A lot of that use was self-mocking, with younger people joking about their own scrolling habits.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: 'Brain rot' named Oxford Word of the Year 2024](https://corp.oup.com/news/brain-rot-named-oxford-word-of-the-year-2024/), [Wikipedia: Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walden)

questions.title: A cooking video puts ketchup on carbonara, and the creator hopes angry comments will push it into more feeds. Which term, Oxford's 2025 Word of the Year, describes it?

options.text: Rage bait
Clickbait
Aura farming
Doomscrolling

questions.explanation:
Oxford defines rage bait as online content deliberately designed to make people angry by being frustrating, provocative or offensive, usually to drive traffic or engagement. Feeds rank posts by engagement, and an angry comment counts as much as a happy one. All the creator needs is replies.

Clickbait is the closest wrong answer. It uses curiosity to get a click ("You won't believe..."), while rage bait uses outrage to get a reaction. *Aura farming*, one of the two words rage bait beat in the final vote, means building a cool image on purpose. More than 30,000 people voted, and Oxford's data showed usage of *rage bait* had tripled in 12 months.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Oxford Word of the Year 2025](https://corp.oup.com/word-of-the-year/)

questions.title: Cambridge Dictionary's 2025 Word of the Year is *parasocial*. Which of these relationships is parasocial?

options.text: A viewer who feels they know a streamer well, although the streamer has never heard of them
Two pen pals who write every week but have never met
Coworkers who only ever talk through a chat app
Friends who met in an online game and play together every night

questions.explanation:
A parasocial relationship is one-sided. One person feels a connection, and the other doesn't know they exist. The wrong answers all happen at a distance or through a screen, but in each one both people know each other and both reply, so none of them is parasocial.

The sociologists Donald Horton and Richard Wohl coined the term in 1956 for TV viewers who felt close to the people on screen. Cambridge picked it for 2025 because the idea has spread from celebrities and influencers to AI chatbots, which people now treat as friends. A chatbot is an odd case: it replies, but nobody on the other side knows you.
questions.references: [Cambridge University Press & Assessment: 'Parasocial' is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2025](https://www.cambridge.org/news-and-insights/parasocial-is-cambridge-dictionary-word-of-the-year-2025), [Wikipedia: Parasocial interaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasocial_interaction)

questions.title: Merriam-Webster chose *slop* as its 2025 Word of the Year. Which meaning earned it the title?

options.text: Low-quality digital content produced in quantity, usually by AI
Food scraps fed to pigs
Soft, wet mud
Overly sentimental writing

questions.explanation:
Merriam-Webster's 2025 definition is "digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence". Think fake news images, junk AI-written books and "workslop" reports that waste coworkers' time.

The other answers are real meanings of *slop*, just older ones. It meant soft mud in the 1700s, food waste by the 1800s, and later anything of little value. The old senses stay in the dictionary while the new one takes over everyday use. Other dictionaries agreed that year: Australia's Macquarie Dictionary chose *AI slop*, and the American Dialect Society chose *slop*.
questions.references: [Merriam-Webster: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/word-of-the-year), [CBS News: "Slop" chosen as Merriam-Webster's 2025 word of the year](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/slop-merriam-webster-2025-word-of-the-year/)

questions.title: Collins picked *vibe coding* as its Word of the Year for 2025. What does it describe?

options.text: Building software by describing what you want in plain language and letting AI write the code
Programming while listening to music to stay in flow
Writing code quickly without a plan, then fixing bugs as they appear
Pair programming where one person talks and the other types

questions.explanation:
Collins defines vibe coding as using AI, prompted by natural language, to help write computer code. You describe the app in plain words, the model writes it, and you judge the result by running it.

"Writing code without a plan" sounds right, because "vibes" suggests improvising. But when you code without a plan, you still type every line yourself. When you vibe code, the AI writes the lines and you may never read them. Collins chose the term because its use grew fast after Andrej Karpathy coined it in a February 2025 post.
questions.references: [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty), [Collins Language Blog: Word of the Year 2025](https://blog.collinsdictionary.com/language-lovers/collins-word-of-the-year-2025-ai-meets-authenticity-as-society-shifts/)

questions.title: Andrej Karpathy coined *vibe coding* in a February 2025 post. What did the post describe?

options.text: Accepting every AI-suggested change without reading the diffs
Forgetting that the code even exists
Using it for throwaway weekend projects
Writing tests first so the AI's code can be trusted
Reviewing every line before it ships

questions.explanation:
Karpathy, an OpenAI cofounder and Tesla's former AI director, wrote about giving in to the vibes and forgetting that the code even exists. He said he clicked "Accept All" and stopped reading the diffs, and that this was fine for throwaway weekend projects. Writing tests and reviewing every line are the opposite of what he described.

The weekend-project limit matters for developers. Simon Willison pointed out that if you review the code an AI writes, test it and can explain how it works, you aren't vibe coding any more. That's ordinary software development. Code nobody has read is fine in a weekend project. In a production system, someone will have to debug it and keep it secure.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Vibe coding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_coding), [Simon Willison: Not all AI-assisted programming is vibe coding](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/19/vibe-coding/)

questions.title: Which of these won Word of the Year at a major English dictionary in 2025?

options.text: Vibe coding
Slop
Parasocial
Rage bait
Rizz
Brain rot
Hallucinate

questions.explanation:
The 2025 winners were *67* (Dictionary.com), *vibe coding* (Collins), *slop* (Merriam-Webster), *parasocial* (Cambridge) and *rage bait* (Oxford). *Rizz* won at Oxford in 2023 and *brain rot* in 2024. *Hallucinate*, in the sense of an AI model confidently making things up, won at both Cambridge and Dictionary.com in 2023.

As the grid shows, the dictionaries rarely pick the same word, because they measure different things. Oxford combines a public vote with its usage data, Cambridge follows what people look up, Collins tracks its language corpus, and Dictionary.com weighs searches, headlines and social media. When different methods agree, as they did on *hallucinate* in 2023, the word was hard to miss.

images.alt: Grid of Words of the Year by dictionary and year. Oxford: rizz in 2023, brain rot in 2024, rage bait in 2025. Merriam-Webster: authentic, polarization, slop. Collins: AI, brat, vibe coding. Cambridge: hallucinate, manifest, parasocial. Dictionary.com: hallucinate, demure, 67. The 2025 column is highlighted.

questions.references: [Wikipedia: Word of the year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_of_the_year), [TIME: 2025's Words of the Year](https://time.com/7334730/word-of-the-year-2025-cambridge-collins-dictionary-oxford-merriam/)

questions.title: Which 2025 winners did their dictionaries link to AI when announcing them?

options.text: Vibe coding (Collins)
Slop (Merriam-Webster)
Parasocial (Cambridge)
Rage bait (Oxford)
67 (Dictionary.com)

questions.explanation:
*Vibe coding* is about AI by definition, and Merriam-Webster's new sense of *slop* names AI-generated content outright. *Parasocial* is the surprise. The word dates from 1956 and television, but Cambridge said its 2025 surge came partly from people forming one-sided bonds with AI chatbots.

*Rage bait* is about human creators and engagement algorithms, not generative AI, and *67* is pure playground. That leaves three of the five big winners tied to AI, and one of them, *vibe coding*, describes how software gets written.
questions.references: [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty), [Merriam-Webster: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.merriam-webster.com/wordplay/word-of-the-year), [Cambridge University Press & Assessment: 'Parasocial' is Cambridge Dictionary's Word of the Year 2025](https://www.cambridge.org/news-and-insights/parasocial-is-cambridge-dictionary-word-of-the-year-2025)

questions.title: Decode this group-chat message. Which definitions fit?
questions.description: > ngl the new intern has zero rizz, but they vibe coded the whole dashboard over the weekend and honestly it's not slop. still weird how parasocial they are about that one tech streamer tho

options.text: *rizz*: charm or social charisma
*vibe coded*: had AI write the code from plain-language prompts
*slop*: low-quality output churned out by AI
*parasocial*: attached to someone who doesn't know they exist
*rizz*: skill at writing code
*parasocial*: good at making friends online

questions.explanation:
The sender says the intern is awkward (no rizz) but built the dashboard by prompting an AI (vibe coded), and the result is surprisingly good (not slop). The last line says the intern feels close to a streamer who has never met them (parasocial).

Both wrong answers come from guessing a word's meaning from its surroundings. In a message about a dashboard, "coding skill" looks like a fit for *rizz*, and the *social* in *parasocial* makes it sound friendly. When a message is about coding, it's easy to assume every word in it is about coding too.
questions.references: [Oxford University Press: Rizz crowned Oxford Word of the Year 2023](https://corp.oup.com/news/rizz-crowned-oxford-word-of-the-year-2023/), [Collins: Word of the Year 2025](https://www.collinsdictionary.com/woty)
